briefing.headline: The simulation predicts that a four-day week on full pay would roughly halve departures over the next 12 months, from 733 to 361 out of 5,000 staff (-48%), but treat that figure as a strong signal of direction, not a forecast.
briefing.most_at_risk: No group reacts badly; caregivers respond most positively (-52% leaving vs -47% for those without caring duties) because a fifth day back eases childcare and eldercare, while managers are the most sceptical voices, expecting the 'same output' promise to land on them first.
risks: Almost every voice, including the most enthusiastic, warns that 'keep output the same' could quietly become five days' work squeezed into four; if that happens, the goodwill could turn into resentment and burnout rather than retention.

This is a six-month trial, but the leaving figure covers 12 months, so it assumes the benefit lasts; several staff say they'll 'believe it when I see it,' and withdrawing the policy at month six could cost more trust than never offering it.
Managers expect to absorb the pressure of hitting output targets with fewer hours, and starting next month leaves little time to plan cover, client expectations and how output will be measured.
design_changes: Before the trial starts, agree with each team how 'output' will be measured, using a small number of concrete measures, and publish them, so staff can see it is not a disguised workload increase.

Give managers time and support to redesign workloads, such as cutting low-value meetings, setting cover rotas for client-facing roles and protecting the day off, and consider pushing the start date back a few weeks to allow this.

Say up front how and when the decision will be made at six months and what happens next, and track hours, workload and wellbeing during the trial, not just output, so a 'yes' or 'no' is based on evidence and does not feel like a cliff edge.
briefing.confidence: low, because the direction is consistent and believable but the size rests on only 48 modelled voices for 5,000 staff, the near-identical effect across every group suggests the model isn't telling groups apart well, and the 12-month figure assumes the policy continues beyond the six-month trial.
